title: Four Knights Sicilian
description: A dynamic and fun Sicilian variation. Pair this course with an Anti-Sicilian repertoire to be ready in e4 c5.

1rbq1rk1/p4ppp/2p1p3/3n4/1b6/2NB4/PPPB1P.text:
The b-file is much better for our rook than the a-file.

A possible maneuver is ...Qc7, ...Bd6 and ...Rd8.

It is an equal position because our centralized knight helps us defend against White's potential attack.

r1b1k2r/ppq2ppp/2n1pn2/1B1p4/1b1NP3/2N1B.text:
We can meet White's threat easily with a great position.

The queen is active on the c-file and eyeing the kingside at the same time.

We'll get castled next, and we also would like to play ...a6 to either force the trade on c6 or play ...b5.

r1bq1rk1/p2n1ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/1b3P2/2N1B3/.text:
But we will castle with a simple plan ahead and a comfortable lead in development.

One idea is ...f6, breaking open the position to the benefit of our better
developed pieces.

The other one is ...c5, taking over the center. We could even implement both of these strong ideas soon.

r1bqk2r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/8/1b2P3/2NBB3/PPP.text:
White still has to worry about the e4-pawn.

Let's strike in the center as planned.

r1bqk2r/p4ppp/2p1p3/3n4/1b6/2NB4/PPPB1PP.text:
The bishop will have to retreat to d2 at some point to keep everything together.

We'll just castle.

We can allow White to trade on d5 as that would bring our pawns back together.

r1bqk2r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/3pP3/1b6/2N1BP2/PPP.text:
White does push e5 now, but this is the wrong approach if we answer correctly.

The most natural retreating square is d7, attacking the e5-pawn.

r1bqk2r/p4ppp/4pn2/3p4/1b6/2NBB3/PPP2PPP.text:
We'll recapture with the c-pawn and connect our pawns.

Castling is next.

After that, we should look to place our rooks on the c- and b-files and put pressure on White's queenside.

An easy position to play.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2N1pn2/8/1b2P3/2N1B3/PP.text:
This trade is not a problem here.

It happens 17% of the time.

We'll recapture with the b-pawn, and ...d5 is coming anyway.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/1b1NP3/2N1BP2/.text:
The most common move in this position is f3, played just over 30% of the time.

Another typical Sicilian move but also another mistake as White continues to fall behind in development.

We'll execute our pawn break.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/1b1NP3/2NBB3/P.text:
The best option to at least develop is Bd3, protecting the pawn that way.

It's played 25% of the time.

We have an easy decision to make, as White has done nothing to prevent ...d5.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2N1p3/3n4/1b6/2NBB3/PPP2P.text:
White can trade.

We'll recapture.

This trade is fine, as they don't have an active knight in the center anymore.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2N1pn2/3p4/1b2P3/2N1BP2/P.text:
White will most likely trade at this point.

The idea is to remove our knight from c6 and push e5, closing the center.

We'll take back, of course, and our center is strong.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3n4/1b1N4/2N1BP2/PP.text:
We can recapture with the knight and White already has to be careful, as multiple pieces are under pressure.

The best course of action for them  is to trade on c6 and then play Bd2.

But we've got a lead in activity even then.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/1B1p4/1b1NP3/2N1BP.text:
A move that might look scary for a moment is 8.Bb5.

White has defended the center with the pawn and now uses their light-squared bishop to apply pressure on our knight and pin it.

But there's nothing to worry about.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3P4/1b1N4/2N1BP2/P.text: Taking on d5 is no good now.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3P4/1b1N4/2NBB3/PP.text:
If they capture, we don't want to recapture with the pawn and leave ourselves with an IQP.

Taking with the knight is more practical.

It puts pressure on White's weak pieces.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PP.text:
Many White players may already be out of book here and start playing "soft" moves such as Be3, which happens 25% of the time.

Although it looks like a reasonable developing move, it does nothing to quell our aggressive central intentions of ...Bb4 and ...d5.

So we'll go for ...Bb4, and the e4-pawn is already under attack.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
White defends, and now we have several choices, but 5...e6 is the Four Knights Sicilian.

Our immediate plan is to continue developing quickly and actively with moves such as ...Bb4 and prepare the ...d5 break.

Generally speaking, the ...d5 pawn break is a major goal for the Black pieces in the Sicilian.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
White strikes in the center.

These are the starting moves of the Open Sicilian, the most popular Sicilian variation.

Almost 50% of games feature the Open Sicilian. That's more than 60 million games in the database!

Let's take.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The knight recaptures.

We'll develop to f6 and attack the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The first knight comes to f3.

We'll develop ours to c6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The 4 Knights Sicilian is exactly what the name says: a Sicilian in which all 4 knights get developed before anything else.

This can lead to positional and "boring" games, but usually makes for an interesting fight as there is a lot of control over the center early.

In Chapter 1, we'll take a look at some of the most common moves at amateur level.

1rb1k2r/p1qp1ppp/4p3/3pP3/1b6/3B4/PPP1QP.text:
We'll continue with ...Rb8, taking the semi-open file.

Castling next is logical, and the bishop can retreat to c5 at some point.

We can even undermine the e5-pawn with ...f6 after we castle, as it would give us the f-file for the rook.

r1b1k2r/p1qp1ppp/4p3/3pP3/1b6/2PB4/PP2QP.text: The natural c3 is a blunder.

r1b1k2r/p1qp1ppp/4p3/3pP3/1b6/3B4/PPP1QP.text:
The best move is Kf1.

White is in no immediate danger but loses castling rights.

r1b1k2r/p1qp1ppp/4p3/3pP3/1b6/3B4/PPPBQP.text:
Bd2 looks like it blocks the check properly, but White will have to move the king anyway.

Because we will capture the bishop and keep an eye on the e5-pawn, so that White can't recapture with the queen.

r1b1k2r/p1qp1ppp/4p3/3pP3/8/2bB4/PP2QPPP.text: We can take the pawn with check, and there's a fork on c3 if White recaptures.

r1b1kb1r/p1qp1ppp/4p3/3pP3/8/3B4/PPP1QPP.text:
White defends with the queen.

But there is a downside to this as well.

We can give a check on b4!

The king has to move. Any alternative is worse than that.

r1b2rk1/p1qp1ppp/4p3/3pP3/8/3B4/PPPKQPPP.text:
But now we have an easy game after castling.

We'll open up the position with a pawn break like ...f6 or ...d6.

White's king is out in the open and this is always better for us.

r1bqk2r/3nbppp/2p1p3/p2pP3/5P2/2NB4/PPP3.text:
And that's to play on the queenside and in the center, where we are the strongest.

Our bishop on c8 is passive so trading it for White's bishop would be great.

Apart from that, we can consider central expansions with ...d4 and ...c5, or placing the knight on c5.

r1bqk2r/p2nbppp/2p1p3/3pP3/5P2/2NB4/PPP3.text:
White players love to grab space like this with tempo.

But we have a viable plan against f4 as well.

r1bqk2r/p3bppp/2p1pn2/3pP3/8/2NB4/PPP2PP.text:
After we play ...d5, e5 is not much of a concern.

We can always retreat to d7 and counterattack the pawn.

r1bqk2r/p4pb1/2p1p3/3p2p1/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
We'll recapture and White's play has only helped us.

The bishop on g7 is strong and the rook is coming to b8.

We have the bishop pair and a lead in activity, not to mention White's non-existent center.

Black is winning.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1p2/2p1p2p/3pP1p1/8/2N3B1/PP.text:
And we'll rotate back to d7 and attack the pawn on e5.

We can continue to pile up on it with ...Bg7 and ...Qc7 if needed.

All in all, we will probably win a pawn with no problems in the position.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/3NP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
8.Nxd5 happens 55% of the time and looks the most natural.

However, we're actually happy to see this trade because it will give us a strong center and a comfortable position.

We have ideas in the long run such as ...d6 to challenge the center or developing the light-squared bishop to a6 in the future.

Our rook should use the b-file which has opened up.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/4P3/8/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
But White's whole idea is e5, which is actually the point of Nxc6. You can expect to see this move over 25% of the time, and likely close to 50% as you climb the rating ladder.

White dominates the d6-square, preventing ...d5.

If White doesn't play e5, our ...d5 idea works against basically any other move.

Our knight was under attack, so we will jump to the center.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/6B1/4P3/2N5/PPP2.text:
Let's show another option that's played 25% of the time, and that's Bg5.

White pins our knight and wants e5 now. Of course, it would be wonderful if this worked.

But we've got ...d5 anyway! This move is essential to play.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/8/4P3/2NB4/PPP2P.text:
White chooses 7.Bd3 nearly 30% of the time.

White prefers the passive route and allow us to achieve a strong center, while they want to castle quickly.

We'll play ...d5, which works every time. If White plays e5 now, simply retreat to d7 and you're fine.

If they take in the center, it's better to recapture with the c-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/4p3/3pP3/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/.text:
White activates the bishop to d3 now and prepares castling.

An immediate idea we could go for is targeting the e5-pawn.

White defending it with f4 would slow down their development and allow ...Bc5, and otherwise the e5-pawn is simply a target.

r1bqkb1r/p4pP1/2p1p3/3p2p1/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text: If White doesn't want to lose a pawn, they will have to continue capturing.

r1bqkb1r/p4pp1/2p1pP1p/3p2B1/8/2N5/PPP2P.text:
White capturing on f6 actually loses the game.

We'll take the bishop, of course.

r1bqkb1r/p4pp1/2p1pn1p/3pP3/7B/2N5/PPP2P.text:
A more sensible move from White is retreating to h4 and keeping the pin.

This forces us to chase the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/4P3/2NB4/PPP2P.text:
White castles instead.

We don't want to take in the center and activate their pieces.

We got our space and it's time to continue developing now.

We'll activate the bishop on e7.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/3pP1B1/8/2N5/PPP2P.text:
It will lead to a sharp line after e5.

White is attacking the pinned knight and we only have one response.

That's to counterattack the bishop on g5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2N1pn2/8/4P3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
It's White capturing on c6, which looks unorthodox because White trades off an active knight in the center for our knight on c6.

It's ambitious, but leads to exciting play, and it's played 20% of the time, in almost 970,000 games at the amateur level.

We'll recapture towards the center. If allowed, ...d5 would be great to play.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
White defends.

And we'll play ...e6 with the plans we already saw in Chapter 1.

Let's take a look at what we have here called "The Ultimate Main Line."

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
White strikes in the center.

Let's take.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White recaptures and there's tension between the knights.

We'll develop the kingside knight first and attack the pawn on e4.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
Activating the knight.

We'll do the same.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Chapter 2 will focus on the main line variations and lines most common at master level.

In particular, the lines including White capturing our knight on move 6 with 6.Nxc6.

It's often designed to push the e-pawn to e5 and try to create some trouble.

Study 1 will take a look at 8.Nxd5.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/3nP3/4N3/8/PPP2PP.text:
In this study, White doesn't trade but rather plays Ne4.

This move is played 33% of the time, in more than 100,000 games.

White wants to completely dominate the d6-square and disallow any ...d6 advancements, with ideas of c4 or Nd6+.

We'll fianchetto, with the idea of ...c5 soon.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/4P3/8/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
And now e5 claims further control of the d6-square.

We'll centralize the knight which was under attack.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2N1pn2/8/4P3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
White will fight against it by capturing first.

We'll recapture.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
White strikes in the center.

Let's capture.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The knight recaptures.

We'll develop our kingside knight and attack e4.

r1r3k1/pb1p1ppp/1q2p3/3n4/2BQ4/1P3P2/PBP.text:
But we can stop it by pinning their queen to the king.

We'll get rid of the queens if White doesn't.

After that, we could consider playing for ...d5.

r1r3k1/pb1p1ppp/3qp3/3n4/2BQ4/1P3P2/PBP3.text: White can threaten mate in one.

r2qkb1r/pb1p1ppp/2p1p3/2P1P3/1n2N3/8/PP3.text:
The best move is probably c5, although it's not the most popular one.

White completely shuts down our bishop on b7 and tries to suffocate our position.

It's crucial to target weaknesses, so I suggest ...Qb8 with an attack on the e5-pawn.

r2qkb1r/pb1p1ppp/2p1p3/3nP3/2P1N3/8/PP3P.text:
The most common and the most logical move is c4, chasing our knight.

We'll jump to b4 rather than b6, and we have a trick up our sleeve if White is persistent.

One option for White here is the immediate Nd6+.

We would neutralize that by taking on d6 and going for ...Qa5 and ...Qe5 ideas.

r2qkb1r/pb1p1ppp/2p1p3/3nP3/4N3/8/PPP1BP.text:
White can choose the calmer route and develop the bishop to e2, preparing castling.

This gives us time to open up our light-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/pb1p1ppp/2p1p3/4P3/1nP1N3/P7/1P3.text:
And they can be persistent with a3.

It might be too passive to retreat to a6 now.

Let's slide the queen to a5 instead and pin the a-pawn to the rook.

The queen is also attacking the e5-pawn.

r2qkb1r/pb1p1ppp/4p3/2pnP3/4N3/8/PPP1BPP.text:
White castles.

And we'll continue improving and attack the pawn on e5.

It actually isn't so straightforward to defend it.

r3k2r/p1qpbppp/4p3/2p1P3/2P1bP2/4B3/PP2B.text:
There is no knight on e4 and we've kept the active bishops.

Now we can begin to undermine their structure with ...d6 and/or ...f6.

r3k2r/p2p1ppp/2pPp3/2P5/1n6/8/PP3PPP/R1B.text:
We'll recapture with the knight which now has an outpost on d5, since White has committed the pawn to c5.

Our pieces will get out via ...f6 and ...Kf7 and we will play against White's extended pawns in the long run.

r3k2r/p2p1ppp/n1pPp3/4P3/1q3P2/8/PP4PP/R.text:
Which we can use to improve the queen here.

Our knight is coming to e4 via c5 and we'll play ...f5 to expand.

White's pawns won't be a huge problem.

r3k2r/pb1p1ppp/2qPp3/2pn4/8/5B2/PPP2PPP/.text:
A sensible defensive effort is Bf3, blocking the diagonal and threatening c4.

We'll prevent it by playing ...c4 ourselves.

It does come with a downside, though.

r3k2r/pb1p1ppp/2qPp3/2pn4/8/5P2/PPP1B1PP.text:
White can choose to defend the king with the pawn.

It does look unnatural compared to Bf3, but White wants c4 anyway.

So let's play it ourselves and prevent them from playing it.

r3k2r/pb1p1ppp/2qPp3/3n4/2pQ4/5B2/PPP2PP.text:
It gives White the d4-square.

We'll castle and defend the kingside.

Now there is an actual threat on the d6-pawn.

r3k2r/pb1p1ppp/2qPp3/3n4/2pQ4/5P2/PPP1B1.text:
White does get to centralize the queen, but the attack on the g7-pawn is easily stopped.

We'll castle, now actually threatening to win the d6-pawn.

r3k2r/pbqp1ppp/3Pp3/2pn4/8/8/PPP1BPPP/R1.text:
The d-pawn recaptures.

White's idea is c4 if we take the pawn on d6, but we don't have to capture it.

We can place the queen on c6 and create a battery on the light squares, aiming towards the king.

r3kb1r/p1qp1ppp/4p3/2p1P3/2P1bP2/4B3/PP2.text: White defends, but we've successfully fought against their setup.

r3kb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/2P1P3/1n2NP2/8/PP4P.text:
We'll take back with the knight, and it's coming to d5.

We will be able to target White's defenses from there.

The bishop will be fine on e7 and we'll castle, also planning for the a-rook to come to b8.

r3kb1r/pb1p1ppp/2p1p3/4q3/1PP1N3/8/1P1B1.text:
This trade is fine.

We'll get a lot of activity.

We'll capture with check.

r3kb1r/pb1p1ppp/2p1p3/4q3/1nP1N3/P4P2/1P.text:
It's probably slightly better for White to avoid the trade of knights.

Our knight has to come back to a6 while theirs stays active in the center.

r3kb1r/pb1p1ppp/2p1p3/8/1PP1q3/8/1P1BBPP.text: The bishop blocking is a big mistake.

r3kb1r/pb1p1ppp/2p1p3/q3P3/1nP1N3/P7/1P1.text:
White pins our knight back.

So we have to capture in the center, counterattacking White's knight.

r3kb1r/pb1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/1PP1q3/8/1P1BBPP.text:
The main point is ...c5, opening up our bishop on b7.

We want to open up our dark-squared bishop as well.

White's space advantage is gone and now we are the ones in the driver's seat.

White's pieces are passive and there are suddenly a lot of problems for them to deal with.

r3kb1r/pb1p1ppp/n1p1p3/4q3/2P1N3/P1B2P2/.text: And they get to improve with Bc3.

r3kb1r/pbqp1ppp/3Np3/2pnP3/8/8/PPP1BPPP/.text:
The best move is to give a check on d6.

We have to take.

r3kb1r/pbqp1ppp/4p3/2p1P3/2P1N3/4B3/PP2B.text:
White has to take because it's a fork.

And we'll take the knight on e4.

The e5-pawn is still under attack.

r3kb1r/pbqp1ppp/4p3/2pnP3/2P1N3/8/PP2BPP.text:
You can expect c4 at any point.

However, when our bishop is on b7 and we've already played ...c5, it's different.

We can sacrifice the knight on e3!

r3kb1r/pbqp1ppp/4p3/2pnP3/4NP2/8/PPP1B1P.text: White could defend it with f4.

r3kb1r/pbqp1ppp/4p3/3nP3/2p1NP2/8/PPP1B1.text:
But ...c4 is a good idea to prevent c4 from White.

The plan is ...Rc8 and then kingside development.

r3kb1r/pbqp1ppp/n1p1p3/8/2P1N3/P1B2P2/1P.text:
Let's retreat to c7 with other ideas in mind.

Now that the e5-pawn is gone, we can look to play ...d5 and ...c5 or ...Nc5 to offer a knight trade.

We will also develop with ...Be7. We have a great position and more central pawns.

r4rk1/pb1p1ppp/1q1Pp3/3n4/2pQ1B2/5B2/PPP.text:
So let's offer a trade of queens.

This will further weaken the d6-pawn and we will be able to play ...f6 and ...e5 to win it.

We should be up a pawn eventually.

r4rk1/pb1p1ppp/2qPp3/3n4/2BQ4/5P2/PPP3PP.text:
We did give up c4 in the process.

But we got rid of the annoying pawn, which was the goal all along.

Looking at the position now, we could continue to play on the queenside with ...Rfc8 and offer a queen trade.

White's queen on d4 is their most active piece.

r4rk1/pb1p1ppp/2qPp3/3n4/2pQ1B2/5B2/PPP2.text:
White defends it with the bishop.

Our queen isn't playing much of a role apart from attacking the pawn.

r4rk1/pb1p1ppp/3qp3/3n4/2BQ4/1P3P2/P1P3P.text:
White goes for b3 now with the goal of Bb2.

Let's occupy the c-file.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
Developing the knight to f3.

We'll activate a knight as well.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
After looking at 8.Nxc6, which could be considered an inaccuracy, let's focus on the best move for White on move 8, which is 8.Ne4.

White logically supports their control of the center and aims for the d6-square.

rq2k2r/p2p1ppp/B1pPp3/2P5/1n6/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
White takes.

We'll recapture with the knight.

White will definitely try to utilize their space advantage.

rq2k2r/p2p1ppp/n1pPp3/2P5/3Q4/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
One such possibility is Qd4 with an attack on g7.

We don't want to castle and allow Bd2, with White basically trapping our pieces.

Let's force a queen trade instead.

This will weaken White's pawns and give us some breathing room.

rq2k2r/p2p1ppp/n1pPp3/4P3/5P2/8/PP4PP/R1.text:
The c-pawn recaptures and White does have a strong pawn chain deep in our camp.

But we have our important open b-file.

rq2k2r/pb1p1ppp/2pPp3/2P5/1n6/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
The d-pawn recaptures.

Those pawns on d6 and c5 do look scary, but we can actually develop around them.

We'll improve our bishop to a6 first and offer a trade, which is one benefit of having our knight on b4.

rq2kb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/2PnP3/4NP2/P7/1P4P.text:
And now we can rotate back to d5 where our knight is safe.

A good plan to continue is ...f5, attacking the knight and blocking the position.

We wouldn't mind White trading with en passant in that scenario.

Did White trick us after Qd4?

Both of our pieces are under attack.

r1bqk2r/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/4P3/1b2n3/2N5/PPPB.text:
If the bishop blocks, we will gladly capture it.

And remove the bishop pair.

r1bqk2r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/4P3/1b6/2N5/PPP1B.text:
The idea is e5.

This time we can jump to e4 when our bishop is already on b4.

r1bqk2r/p2p2pp/2p1pp2/4P3/1b6/2N5/PPPQBP.text:
And now we can begin to challenge White's structure, with castling in mind.

11.exf6 Qxf6 and our queen is out. 

White lacks central pawns in this variation, which means we'll control the center after we play ...d5.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2N1p3/8/4n3/2P5/P1P1BPP.text:
White can trade on c6 now.

It's different when the center is open and I advise against recapturing with the b-pawn.

White would have the strong Qd4.

Let's take with the d-pawn instead and offer a trade of queens.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2N1pn2/8/1b2P3/2N5/PPP1.text:
White can choose to trade here, similar to the main line of the Four Knights Sicilian.

This happens 25% of the time.

We'll recapture with the b-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/8/3Nn3/2PB4/P1P2P.text:
White can also play the dangerous Bd3.

Don't go pawn grabbing here and run into Qg4.

It's much more important to develop and consolidate after already winning a pawn.

Let's protect the knight instead.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/8/3Nn3/2PQ4/P1P1B.text:
The most common move at this point is Qd3.

White attacks our knight on e4 and defends the c3-pawn.

It's much more active to defend the knight with ...d5 than move it away.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/1b1NP3/2N2P2/P.text: 7.f3 is played 24% of the time and runs into ...d5.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/1b1NP3/2N5/PPP.text:
A move that's played 18% of the time but has by far the most independent value is 7.O-O.

It's actually best for White to sacrifice the pawn on e4! They will look for compensation in activity and the strong bishops.

We will take them up on their offer.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/3NP3/2P5/P1P1B.text:
The pawn recaptures.

And we'll grab a pawn in the center.

Let's see White's options on how to approach this position where they've sacrificed a pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/4p3/3p4/3Nn3/B1PQ4/P1P1B.text:
We can block the bishop immediately and castle on the next move.

White might want c4 at some point,  which you shouldn't be afraid of. 

Letting White capture and playing with an IQP is fine.

Of course, ...Re8 is one short-term goal to unpin the knight on e7.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3p4/3Nn3/B1PB4/P1P2.text:
White prevents castling for a while.

It's important to waste no time here but try to castle as quickly as possible.

We can attack that bishop immediately, as well as the pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3p4/3Nn3/B1PQ4/P1P1.text:
Don't be scared of Ba3.

White won't prevent us from castling for a long time.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/1b1NP3/2N2P2/P.text:
We get to expand in the center, unbothered.

8.exd5 Nxd5 puts pressure on c3 and we have a small edge. 

We also have ...Qa5 ideas, and we enjoy a comfortable position. White has to be careful not to lose a pawn!

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/2n5/6Q1/2PB4/P1P2PP.text:
It's dangerous to do it now if White plays Qg4.

The g7-pawn is under attack.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/4n3/2PB4/P1P2PPP/.text:
White can decline and place the bishop on d3.

Let's rotate the knight to c5 and prepare castling.

We would like to capture on d3 at some point.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP1.text:
White activates the bishop 7% of the time, and it was played in more than 310,000 games.

This is a natural developing move after all, and whether it's good or bad will depend on White's follow-up.

Let's pin the knight on c3. Now the e4-pawn is under pressure and White has to make an important decision regarding this pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Two pawns in the center.

Let's capture.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The knight recaptures.

We'll attack the center.

r2k3r/p2b1ppp/2p1p3/1p1n4/8/2P2BB1/P1P2P.text:
This means that ...b5 is useful to prevent c4.

We'll connect the rooks with ...Ke7 next and figure out how to play against White's bishops and reach an endgame.

All in all, an equal position.

r2k3r/pp1b1ppp/2p1p3/3n4/8/2P2BB1/P1P2PP.text:
White retreats to g3.

Again, capturing on c3 isn't necessary here.

It's better to try and keep our knight on d5 instead.

r2k3r/pp1b1ppp/2p1pn2/8/5B2/2P2B2/P1P2PP.text:
As mentioned, White is banking on their strong bishops.

We'll attack one of them immediately.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White activates the knight.

We'll do the same.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
This study will focus on another 6th move alternative for White, which is 6.Be2.

I call it tricky because it seems like a calm and normal developing move, but White often follows it up with a vicious pawn sacrifice!

Let's take a look.

r1b1k2r/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/4P3/1bB4q/2N5/PPPB.text:
And we have the fork on h4, taking advantage of the misplaced bishop on c4.

A winning position for us.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3q4/3N4/P3B3/1PP2P.text:
So they protect the knight instead.

Here, we can develop with ...Be7 or ...Bd7 and it's a fine position.

Also good, but a little boring, is the next line, capturing in the center.

But we will show that line as well.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/3q4/3Q4/P3B3/1PP2PPP.text:
White recaptures with the queen.

We'll trade.

r1bqk2r/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/4P3/1bB1n3/2N5/PPP.text:
For example, Bd2 is a blunder, although it seems natural.

We can capture on f2!

r1bqk2r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/4P3/1bB5/2N5/PPP2.text:
White can attack our knight, but it's slightly different than the main lines.

We can utilize the pin on c3 and prepare to bring the queen to a5 to help out with the attack.

White's best move is Qg4 here.

r1bqk2r/p2p1ppp/2p1pn2/8/1bB1P3/2N5/PPPB.text:
White can defend with the bishop.

Our plans stay the same.

We'll strike in the center. White is facing the typical central problems.

r1bqk2r/p4ppp/4pn2/3p4/1bB5/2N5/PPPB1PPP.text:
We'll recapture with the c-pawn and keep our powerful pawn chain in the center.

If White gives a check on b5, we will block with the bishop.

Otherwise, castling and ...Bb7 is strong. White gave us everything we wanted.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/2N1pn2/8/1bB1P3/2N5/PPP.text:
White takes on c6 first.

We'll recapture with the b-pawn, as per usual.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP.text:
The c4-square is simply a silly square for the bishop, as it directly runs into all of our ideas.

You will face this move 5% of the time, and it was played in just under 250,000 games.

We'll pin the knight first, reintroducing the threat on e4 with the idea of ...d5, of course.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/3NP3/2N3P1/PP.text:
This option is not bad compared to White's other moves and some players enjoy playing fianchetto ideas.

Here, it's only played 1% of the time, though.

Still, it does nothing to stop our plan in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/3NP3/P1N5/1PP.text:
6.a3 is only played 3% of the time, probably because it's slow.

However, it does take care of ...Bb4.

The direct execution of our main idea is ...d5, so that's the simplest continuation here.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
The knight comes out to c3 and defends.

We'll play ...e6 with the standard plans ahead.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3N4/3N4/P7/1PP2PPP.text:
White takes.

Now we'll finally recapture with the queen.

It's not good for White to trade off their active knight.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/1B1p4/3NP3/P1N5/1.text:
You could also expect Bb5 at a certain frequency.

White players love to pin the knights like this when there's already tension between them.

We'll simply unpin and defend.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3P4/3N4/2N3P1/PPP.text:
White takes.

We'll recapture. We now have an IQP.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3P4/3N4/P1N5/1PP2.text:
It's natural for White to take in the center.

If we recapture with the pawn, we'll get an IQP.

So let's recapture with the knight instead, playing actively!

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/3p4/3N4/2N3P1/PPP2.text:
Which is convenient for White to attack with Bg2.

Most of the play will revolve around this pawn.

But we have a tricky move now. We can activate the bishop to g4 with tempo!

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
White strikes in the center.

Let's capture that pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The knight recaptures.

We'll attack the center.

r2q1rk1/pp1bbppp/2n2n2/1B1p4/3N4/P1N5/1P.text:
But we can unpin immediately by castling.

Having almost finished development, it's time to improve next.

We'll do that with ...a6, ...Re8 and ...Rc8.

Both sides have easy development although White is slightly more active.

r2q1rk1/pp1bbppp/2n2n2/3p4/3N4/2N2PP1/PP.text:
And we'll castle, with active plans ahead.

The rooks are coming to e8 and c8 and the bishop will improve to either c5 or b4.

We should focus on protecting the IQP in the long run.

r2qk2r/pp1bbppp/2n2n2/1B1p4/3N4/P1N5/1PP.text: The rook pins our bishop on the e-file.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2bp4/3N2b1/2NQB1P1/P.text:
Instead, they can choose to keep the knight on d4 and continue developing.

We will insist.

The queen is attacking the b2-pawn as well.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2n1pn2/1B1P4/3N4/P1N5/1.text:
White captures in the center once.

We'll take back.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2n2n2/1B1p4/3N4/P1N5/1P.text:
White castles.

We can prepare to do the same.

A calm game.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2n2n2/3p4/3N4/2N2PP1/PP.text:
So they resort to castling.

Let's develop the other bishop as well, preparing castling ourselves.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/3p4/3N2b1/2N2PP1/PP.text:
Provoking f3 is basically what we wanted.

We'll retreat, and now White's bishop isn't active anymore.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/3p4/3N2b1/2NQ2P1/PP.text:
White escapes to d3. They had to keep an eye on the knight on d4.

Let's put more pressure on it now.

We are happy to see White trade on c6 at any point.

r3k2r/p4ppp/2p2n2/3p4/6b1/2N1P1P1/PPP3BP.text:
Now our pawns are back together and White has an obvious weakness on e3.

We will play against this target next.

I'm sure this is not what White had hoped for at the beginning of the game.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/1qN2n2/2bp4/6b1/2NQB1P1/PPP.text:
White is basically forced to trade now.

I suggest we take on e3 first.

We don't want to allow White to trade on c5.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/1qN2n2/3p4/6b1/2N1Q1P1/PPP2.text:
The queen recaptures.

The whole point of these trades is to create a big weakness.

r3kb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/8/3B4/P7/1PP2PPP/R3K.text:
And now we can bring our bishop to d7 with the idea of ...Bc6, where the bishop will be strong.

White's bishop on d4 is good, but we can neutralize it with ...Rg8.

Both sides have a pawn majority they can use in the endgame.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The knight comes out to f3.

We'll develop our knight, too.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
It's time to look at the rarest of sidelines White can choose to play on move 6, which are 6.Bc4, 6.a3 and 6.g3.

These are far from optimal and we should get good positions by sticking to basic principles we've learned in this course.

If anything, this will be a display of why and how the recommended moves are exceptionally strong against the "bad" sidelines.

1rb1kb1r/p1qn1ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/5B2/2NB4/PP.text:
They defend with the queen.

Our queen is convenient on c7 because we can target the pawn with ...f6.

White can't capture because the pawn is pinned.

1rbk1b1r/p1qn2pp/2p1pp2/3pP2Q/5B2/2NB4/P.text:
But our king is actually safe on d8 and now White can't save the pawn on e5.

We'll take it with the knight and already reach an advantage that can't be dismissed.

This whole line was us targeting weaknesses and White defending.

That's what happens when you don't play your opening in the best way.

1rbqkb1r/p2n1ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/5B2/2NB4/PPP.text:
White defends.

But they will have to react one more time because we are attacking the pawn on e5.

r1bqkb1r/3n1ppp/2p1p3/p2pP3/5P2/2NB4/PPP.text:
And we'll go ...a5, with a lot of ideas in mind.

They are to push ...d4 and/or ...c5 and ...c4. The c5-square is also a good square for the knight.

We can trade the light-squared bishops on a6 and play ...Be7 to prepare castling.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/5B2/2NB4/PPP.text:
White brings the bishop to d3.

Before anything else, we can demonstrate how to make use of the b-file.

r1bqkb1r/p2n1ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/5P2/2NB4/PPP.text: The bishop comes out between the pawns.

r1bqkb1r/p2npppp/2p1P3/3p4/8/3B4/PPP2PPP.text:
Nope! Their whole idea is e6!

We can't capture on e6 as that would lead to a quick checkmate for White.

Let's bring the knight to e5 instead.

r1bqkb1r/p2npppp/2p5/3pP3/5B2/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
Defending with the bishop is not the best option.

It's going to be passive in the long run and it leaves the defense of the b2-pawn.

We can block the pawn first and prepare to harass b2 with the queen at some point.

r1bqkb1r/p2npppp/2p5/3pP3/5P2/2N5/PPP3PP.text:
It's better to protect the pawn with f4.

We'll block White's structure.

r1bqkb1r/p2ppppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
White defends the pawn now almost 45% of the time.

But one can argue that the trade on c6 was unnecessary if this was their plan all along.

So we'll strike in the center.

r1bqkb1r/p2ppppp/2p2n2/8/4P3/3B4/PPP2PPP.text:
Let's look at a funny line White can go for here.

6.Bd3 is played more than 25% of the time. White is awaiting ...d5 and has a plan.

We'll play it. Expanding in the center is essential.

r1bqkb1r/p3pPpp/2p5/3pn3/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/R.text:
So that once White captures on f7...

We can recapture with the knight.

r1bqkb1r/p3pppp/2p2n2/3P4/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
It's much more frequent for White to capture on d5 here than push e5.

We'll recapture, of course.

When both the b- and the c-pawns are missing, you should expect some pressure on the e8-a4 diagonal.

r1bqkb1r/p3pppp/2p2n2/3pP3/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
White can try to push here.

We'll attack the pawn.

They can't play e6 like in the 6.Bd3 line because there is no bishop on d3.

r1bqkb1r/p3pppp/2p2n2/3pP3/8/3B4/PPP2PPP.text:
White wanted to push e5 the whole time.

We'll retreat to d7 and attack the pawn.

What now? Will White play f4 or Bf4 to protect the pawn?

r1bqkb1r/p3pppp/5n2/1B1p4/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
White gives a check on the b5-square.

We'll block with the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/p4npp/2p1p3/3p4/8/3B4/PPP2PPP/R.text:
And we'll play ...e6 ourselves.

This is a ridiculous line but I'd say we come out on top with the important central presence.

We'll develop naturally next.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/4P3/4BP2/PPP3P.text:
We can just recapture on c6 and keep our strong pawns in the center.

White now has the unnecessary pawn on f3 and we already have a slight advantage.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/2PNP3/5P2/PP4.text: Even if White goes for c4...

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/8/3NP3/4BP2/PPP.text:
Let's demonstrate how strong our plans are if White plays a natural but soft move like Be3.

We can strike in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2N2n2/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
We are generally happy to see this trade because we can strengthen our center and open up the b-file.

5.Nxc6 is played 20% of the time, and it was seen in more than 2 million games!

So we'll recapture with the b-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/8/3NP3/5P2/PPP3P.text:
5.f3 is only played 2% of the time here. It does protect the e4-pawn, but doesn't fight for the center.

We are ahead in development and are ready to strike with ...d5 and/or develop actively with ...Bc5 to exploit the g1-a7 diagonal.

It was also definitely possible to immediately attack with 5...d5!

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2N1pn2/3p4/4P3/4BP2/PPP3.text: Capturing on c6 doesn't really help White.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/2PNP3/5P2/PP4.text:
We can still play ...d5.

This will open up the center and give us easy development and activity.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
White strikes in the center.

We'll take.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The knight recaptures.

We'll attack the pawn. All standard so far.

r2qkb1r/p2Bpppp/5n2/3p4/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
White trades.

No problem. We'll recapture with the queen.

r3kb1r/p2q1ppp/4pn2/3p4/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
Pretty standard and easy development for both sides.

We connect the pawn chain and prepare ...Be7 and ...O-O.

The rook will occupy the semi-open b-file and we'll enjoy a comfortable position.

We could even bring the kingside rook to the c-file and dominate the queenside.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The standard continuation.

We'll get our piece out, too.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In the sixth chapter of this course, we will analyze White's sidelines already on move 5.

The most logical move is of course 5.Nc3 to defend the e4-pawn, but what if White doesn't play that?

Viable options could also be 5.Nxc6 and 5.f3. Let's see.
